text:
The doorbell camera pings at 3:12 every night.

I work the overnight shift at the county hospital, so my telephone stays in my pocket with the volume turned all the way up. The notification arrives whether I am at work or at home, and it is never early or late. It is a bright electronic chime, like a spoon tapped against a glass.

The first night, I was sitting in the staff room during my break, eating crackers from a vending machine. I opened the application expecting a delivery driver or a wandering cat, but I found a recording eleven seconds long instead.

A motionless figure stood on my porch in a dark gray hood, facing away from the entrance. The shoulders never moved, and the hands hung heavily at the sides. There was no wind and no sound, and the figure never turned around, not even once. I watched it three times, and then I laughed, because laughing was easier than the alternative.

Obviously somebody was playing a joke on me. I live alone in a small suburban house at the end of a quiet street, and I am the kind of person who waves at everybody. Perhaps a bored teenager had borrowed a sweatshirt, or perhaps the camera had a technical problem. I deleted the recording and finished my crackers.

The next night the chime came again, and so did the figure, and by the fourth night I had stopped laughing completely.

On the ninth morning I drove home at dawn, tired and cold, while the sun came up pink behind the rooftops. I parked in the driveway and walked toward my porch, where the boards were dry, because it had not rained for a week.

But across the boards there were footprints, wet and bare, shining in the early light. They crossed the whole porch and stopped at my front door. None of them led away.
summary: The narrator, a night-shift nurse, gets a doorbell camera alert at 3:12 every night showing a hooded figure on her porch; after nine nights she finds wet bare footprints that lead to her front door and none that lead away.
